name: Nawatl de Orizaba / de la Sierra de Zongolica, Rafael Delgado variety

catalog_locator: Lección 1, §1.2 'Estructura Silábica y Acentuación', recuadro 'Acento penúltimo (grave) o escrito', and nota [10]; exception classes (pp. 44-46)
catalog_quote: La acentuación del náhuatl es casi siempre penúltima (grave), es decir se acentúa la sílaba anterior a la última de la palabra. Aunque sea muy larga la palabra, (y puede tener acentos secundarios), el acento principal siempre cae sobre esa sílaba. Por ejemplo, Ōtikoninmoopōchīxtololotatakaltilihtikīsaskiāya Ud. (forma reverencial) de repente les habría hecho rascarse el ojo izquierdo se pronuncia con un solo acento fuerte, sobre la ā. Por lo tanto, las palabras con acento penúltimo no llevarán acento escrito.[10] Algunas variantes, entre ellas la de Orizaba, tienen palabras con otro acento: esas sí se representarán en este libro con acento escrito (p.ej. pakílistli alegría, ihkón así), aunque en la ortografía normal de la región ni en esos casos se escribe el acento. ... [10] Dado que, como ya indicamos, dos vocales consecutivas pertenecen a diferentes sílabas, cuando se encuentran a final de palabra, se acentúa la primera, aunque no lleve acento escrito. Esto a veces choca con las convenciones del español, donde tal secuencia se interpretaría como diptongo. P.ej. kitlalia lo pone se acentúa como la voz española valía, no como Italia, es decir, se pronuncia [kitlalía], no *[kitlálya].
world_status: statement found in an open source

Aunque sea muy larga la palabra, (y puede tener acentos secundarios), el acento principal siempre cae sobre esa sílaba. [...] Por lo tanto, las palabras con acento penúltimo no llevarán acento escrito. Algunas variantes, entre ellas la de Orizaba, tienen palabras con otro acento: esas sí se representarán en este libro con acento escrito (p.ej. pakílistli alegría, ihkón así), aunque en la ortografía normal de la región ni en esos casos se escribe el acento.
new_statements.translation: Nahuatl stress is almost always penultimate ('grave'), i.e. the syllable before the last one of the word is stressed. However long the word (and it may have secondary stresses), the main stress always falls on that syllable. [...] Therefore words with penultimate stress will carry no written accent. Some varieties, among them that of Orizaba, have words with a different stress: those will be represented in this book with a written accent (e.g. pakílistli 'joy', ihkón 'thus'), although in the normal orthography of the region the accent is not written even in those cases.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (cp1252 HTML, Tuggy 1991/2004 Lecciones, Leccion 1). Under heading '1.2 Estructura Silabica y Acentuacion', sidebar 'Acento penultimo (grave) o escrito', the quoted passage is present word for word: 'La acentuacion del nahuatl es casi siempre penultima (grave), es decir se acentua la silaba anterior a la ultima de la palabra. Aunque sea muy larga la palabra, (y puede tener acentos secundarios), el acento principal siempre cae sobre esa silaba.' followed by the long reverential verb example 'se pronuncia con un solo acento fuerte, sobre la a [long a]' (the part the compilers elided with [..]), then 'Por lo tanto, las palabras con acento penultimo no llevaran acento escrito.[10]…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, regardless of word length; a word-final vowel sequence counts as two syllables, so stress falls on the first of the two vowels (kitlalía). Orizaba Nawatl has a lexically/morphologically defined minority of words with non-penultimate stress (antepenult e.g. pakílistli, final e.g. ihkón), which Tuggy marks with a written accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Tuggy notes long words 'puede tener acentos secundarios' (may have secondary stresses) but gives no placement rule; only one strong (main) stress per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Tuggy: some Orizaba words have other stress (pakílistli antepenult, ihkón final). Jerónimo Sánchez 2012 (pp. 44-46, same town, Rafael Delgado) details them: most nouns of more than three syllables with absolutive -li/-tli are antepenult-stressed (áhawilli, íchpochtli, mikílistli, póballi, télpochtli; exception itskwintli penult); verbs in -tia (kiawiltía, kikixtía), some adjectives in -Vk (tliliwík, chikawák), oksé 'other', ihkón 'thus' are final-stressed; Spanish oxytone loans are nativized with final -n and regular penult stress (café > kahwen, SIL /h/ final page).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('la sílaba anterior a la última de la palabra'), illustrated on isolated citation forms including a very long polysynthetic verb word pronounced with a single main stress; no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Tuggy's Lecciones describes specifically the speech of Rafael Delgado (San Juan del Río), Veracruz, a sub-variety of Orizaba/Sierra de Zongolica Nawatl (oriz1235, nlv); Jerónimo Sánchez 2012 describes the same town (RD). Both fall under Glottolog oriz1235; no separate dialect glottocode known.

new_statements.quote: In stressed (penultimate, usually) position, vowels tend to be lengthened, as the following chart of average lengths of (historically) short vowels indicates. [...] Total | 51 (54) | 92 (12) | 80% [...] In general the stressed vowels seem to be longer than their neighbors, irrespective of whether they were historically long or short. [...] Otherwise the longest vowels in each word are stressed vowels [Sec. V]. [Sec. I, quoting Goller et al. 1974:] "Length does not appear to carry the same functional load that it carries in other Nahuatlan languages. This load may prove to be carried by stress in Orizaba Nahuatl."

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog (penult) and as Tuggy 1991's 'casi siempre penúltima'; adds the phonetic correlate (stressed vowels lengthened ~80%, stress overriding historical vowel length in discourse) and repeats Goller et al. 1974's suggestion that stress rather than length carries the functional load. The 'usually' hedge matches the 'casi siempre' of the existing statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable ('penultimate, usually'); the paper is about vowel length, not stress, and mentions placement only in passing. Its instrumental finding is that stressed (penult) short vowels are on average about 80% longer than unstressed ones (92 vs 51 msec) and that in running speech the stressed vowel is the longest in the word regardless of historical length.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually' in 'penultimate, usually'; no exceptions are listed.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper describes the Nahuatl of Rafael Delgado, Veracruz (the catalog's variety), from two male native speakers, Victor Hernández de Jesús (41) and Juan Carrasco (25), recorded by Jeff Burnham in Orizaba; the page places RD in the Orizaba Nawatl dialect area (ISO nlv). The 2008 web version lists the authors as Burnham & Tuggy; Tuggy's CV files it as Tuggy 1979c 'con Jeff Burnham'.

sources.note: No mention of tone, pitch or intonation anywhere in the page (checked: 'tono', 'entonación' absent). Word prosody is described entirely as stress accent: default penultimate ('acento grave'); a word-final two-vowel sequence is two syllables with stress on the first vowel (niktlalía); systematic ANTEPENULTIMATE stress in words of 3+ syllables ending in C-tli / l-li (absolutive: tépostli, tláxkalli; but -tzin-tli stressed on -tzin, and piltzintli, itzkuintli etc. penultimate), C-tih (plural), C-ki (preterite sg / nominalizer; except o-/yo- past verbs of three syllables), C-ko (locative); FINAL…

tone.quote: El acento grave es el que cae sobre la penúltima sílaba de la palabra. La gran mayoría de las palabras del nawatl son graves, con las excepciones mencionadas adelante. Cuando la palabra termina con dos vocales, el acento cae sobre la primera de ellas. Por ejemplo, niktlalia ‘lo pongo’ tiene el acento sobre la (segunda) i. [...] En los siguientes tipos de palabras, con tal que la palabra tenga al menos tres sílabas, es eesdrújula [sic], o sea, su acento cae sobre la sílaba antepenúltima. [...] Palabras que terminan en: [...] C-tli o l-li, donde -tli/-li es el sufijo absolutivo. [...] Hay unas cuantas palabras que son agudas (el acento cae en la última sílaba).
tone.locator: web page (unpaginated), section 'Sílabas y acento': subsections 'La regla general: Acento grave', 'Acento esdrújulo', 'Acento agudo'
tone.translation: The 'grave' accent is the one that falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. The great majority of Nawatl words are penultimately stressed, with the exceptions mentioned below. When the word ends in two vowels, the accent falls on the first of them. For example, niktlalia 'I put it' has the accent on the (second) i. [...] In the following types of words, provided the word has at least three syllables, it is antepenultimately stressed, i.e. its accent falls on the antepenultimate syllable. [...] Words that end in: [...] C-tli or l-li, where -tli/-li is the absolutive suffix. [...] There are a few words that are finally stressed (the accent falls on the last syllable).
